rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. Moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to identify which crowded pairs respond to slope. The initial last peak at 6.31 minutes leaves room to spread the cluster without approaching the acquisition limit.
Keep the improved shallow slope and test higher temperature to shift the remaining close pair's selectivity. Reduced retention may also bring the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test the midpoint temperature: the critical cluster changes substantially between 40 and 60 C, suggesting an intermediate temperature may avoid both co-elutions. Preserve the shallow slope that resolved most pairs.

At 60 C only one pair remains unresolved, and its different peak widths suggest differing responses to gradient slope. A modestly steeper gradient tests whether that co-elution can be separated while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Shorten the gradient one step to continue separating the remaining critical pair, whose resolution improved markedly at 20 minutes. This tests whether it reaches 1.5 before the earlier pair, currently at 1.61, becomes limiting.

The best run is nearly fully resolved. Raising the starting organic fraction one step slightly shallows the gradient and shifts selectivity, testing whether the pair at R = 1.46 can reach baseline resolution without losing separation elsewhere.

Use a slope of 0.0458 organic fraction per minute, slightly shallower than injection 7, to improve its two marginal early pairs while preserving the later pair's resolution margin. The final organic fraction remains well above the observed elution window.

Slightly reduce the slope from 0.0458 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the marginal early pairs above R = 1.5 while retaining the later pair's small margin. The last peak should remain inside the gradient and below 10 minutes.

Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF; now test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten elution while keeping it as the benchmark. The resulting shallower slope may compensate for compression of the early critical pairs.

Test whether a 5 C temperature decrease restores the early critical pair in the shorter method, while monitoring the neighboring pair for a selectivity crossover. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

With the maximum CRF secured, explore a lower-temperature selectivity regime that may permit a faster, steeper gradient without the high-temperature critical pairs. The broad final solvent strength guards against late elution.

Test a steeper gradient in the low-temperature regime to shift the lone unresolved pair and shorten the run. Comparing directly with injection 12 will reveal whether this selectivity regime can support a faster fully resolved method.

Hold the faster gradient fixed and lower temperature one step to move the remaining co-eluting pair away from its crossover. Most other pairs have enough resolution margin to make this a useful test of a shorter fully resolved method.

Test a substantially higher starting organic fraction to shorten the low-temperature separation and shift the persistent close pair through a different solvent window. Injection 9 remains the fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.

Test a steeper gradient to move the broad member of the unresolved pair further past its neighbor, following the crossover seen in the low-temperature scouting runs. This could yield a substantially faster separation, although the next pair may become limiting.

Combine an intermediate slope with lower temperature to improve spacing across the central three-peak cluster. Monitor the late pair closely, since cooling reduced its resolution in the earlier scouting runs; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Shift the solvent window upward while preserving injection 17's slope to test whether starting composition can resolve its two marginal pairs and shorten elution. The first peak was still well retained, leaving room to raise the starting organic fraction.

Shallow injection 18's gradient to improve the pairs at R = 1.02 and 1.40, using the central pair's R = 2.19 as a margin against compression. This targets full resolution with substantially earlier final elution than injection 9.
Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten retention, paired with a shallower slope to protect the critical central and late pairs. Injection 19 is now the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the temperature one step from the faster fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without sacrificing its critical central pair. Keep injection 19 as the benchmark if resolution falls below 1.5.

Test a small slope increase from 0.050 to 0.055 organic fraction per minute to locate the speed limit near injection 19. This should shorten elution, but the pair previously at R = 1.61 may become limiting.

Lower the starting fraction one step from injection 19 while modestly increasing slope to test a different balance of the central pair spacings. This targets another fully resolved method with potentially better resolution margins; injection 19 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Slightly shallow the fastest fully resolved method to strengthen its two smallest resolution margins while keeping final elution well below 10 minutes. This tests a more robust maximum-score alternative to injection 19.

Trim injection 19's gradient duration while preserving its starting composition and slope, which achieved full resolution with the last peak at 4.14 minutes. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, so all peaks should retain their separation while unnecessary gradient programming is removed.
